[p.40] The contour boundaries marked by /+/ delimit sequences of phonation which will be called phonemic words. ... Each phonemic word, then, is preceeded and followed by pause or potential pause and consists of one contour with only one prominent syllable of higher pitch and primary stress. The location of the pitch and stress within the phonemic word bounded by /+/ is determined by the structure of the syllable and its position relative to the juncture. Syllables are of three structural grades, determined by the presence or absence of length and semi-vowels. Light syllables contain short vowels not followed by a semi-vowel. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable: within the phonemic word (bounded by plus juncture) primary stress and high pitch fall on the first syllable, unless the second syllable outranks it on a three-grade weight scale (light CV < heavy CV+semivowel < extra-heavy CV: long vowel), in which case the second syllable is stressed; a two-syllable left-edge window. Examples: [kírim] 'cat (obj.)', [máyum] 'feet (obj.)', but [holówa] 'to scare someone', [lilé·] 'to accuse', [ciyí·ya] 'to be all squashed up'. A word-internal hyphen juncture (after a few prefixes, in some compounds, before some auxiliaries) restarts the computation from the hyphen, the pre-hyphen part taking only secondary stress by the same first-unless-second-heavier rule. Separately, a phonemic phrasal accent /'/ (very high pitch, extra-heavy stress) of unpredictable location falls on one of the prominent syllables of a phrase (sec. 1.2, p. 47).
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'A weaker, or secondary stress, occurs on any heavy syllable following the prominent syllable and varies in intensity, being proportionately stronger as that syllable is further from the preceding prominent syllable' (p. 41); material preceding a word-internal hyphen juncture carries only secondary stress, placed on its first syllable unless its second is heavier (p. 44-45).
new_statements.exceptions: Hyphen juncture shifts the locus (prefix + stem, compounds, auxiliaries/enclitics). Dialect/idiolect variation: Schlichter 1981: 5-6 and Shepherd 2005: 2 report that Grace McKibbin (Hayfork Wintu) had no hyphen juncture and did not shift stress to a heavier second syllable, so all her words were stressed on the first syllable except under contrastive/special emphasis and in some exclamations; Pitkin's rule describes McCloud Wintu (main informant Carrie Dixon) and also held for Renee Coleman.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonemic word' delimited by plus juncture /+/, which Pitkin equates with informant citation words; stress is analysed as a predictable component of juncture, not a phoneme; phrase-level 'phrasal accent' is a separate, contrastive suprasegmental. The 1984 published grammar (UCPL 94) is the revised version of this dissertation; its inventory page (p. 25, Rosetta excerpt on file) likewise lists only junctures and phrasal accent as suprasegmentals.
new_statements.identity_note: Pitkin 1963/1984 describes primarily McCloud River Wintu (main informant Carrie B. Dixon; rule also holds for Renee Coleman per Schlichter 1981). Hayfork (Upper Trinity) Wintu as spoken by Grace McKibbin is reported (Schlichter 1981: 5-6; Shepherd 2005: 2) to have plain word-initial stress with no weight-driven shift and no hyphen juncture. All are Wintu proper, glottocode wint1259 (not Nomlaki noml1242 or Patwin patw1250).

sources.note: Sec. 110, p. 2: McKibbin (Hayfork) lacked Pitkin's hyphen juncture (Pitkin 1984: 20-21); 'In McKibbin's pronunciation, stress is always on the first syllable of a word, even if it is a prefix, with the exception of occasional special emphasis and some exclamation words.'

sources.citation: Schlichter [Shepherd], Alice. 1981. Wintu Dictionary. Reports from the Survey of California and Other Indian Languages, Report 2. Berkeley: Dept. of Linguistics, UC Berkeley. (eScholarship item 47v2w4gw; scan without text layer, front matter pp. 2-16 scanned)
sources.note: Introduction pp. 5-6: follows Pitkin 1963's hyphen-juncture rules, which hold for speakers Renee Coleman and Carrie Dixon; 'Grace MacKibben uses primary not secondary stress on morphemes preceding hyphen juncture and does not move the stress from the first to a heavier second syllable--except for contrastive purposes--so that in her speech all words are stressed on the first syllable.'
Paraphrases Pitkin: prominent syllable is the first unless the second is heavier; used only to locate the eScholarship IDs (tertiary).
